name: Learn: AppArmor Confinement
objective: CKS › System Hardening (15%). Drill EVERY AppArmor corner harder than the exam: write + load a profile on a node with apparmor_parser, understand profile-name vs filename, reference it from a pod via the typed appArmorProfile field (Localhost / RuntimeDefault / Unconfined), prove a denied write is blocked, contrast confined vs unconfined, load a second stricter profile, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix for a pod stuck on a missing profile. Graded exactly, per requirement.
description: Eight strict AppArmor practicals on a real multi-node cluster. Profiles are written and loaded on worker node $W1 via apparmor_parser; pods reference them with securityContext.appArmorProfile. Each Check shows which requirements you met and the exact reason for any you missed.

questions.title: Write and load a deny-write profile on a node
questions.teach:
**AppArmor** is a Linux Security Module giving path-based **Mandatory Access Control**: a profile names rules like `deny /etc/secret-data/** w,` to block writes under a path. Load it on the node with `apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/<file>` (`-W` waits for completion).

**Gotcha:** the kernel tracks a profile by its **profile name** (the string after the `profile` keyword), not the filename — pods reference that name, so keep file and name matching.
questions.prompt:
On worker node `$W1`, write an AppArmor profile file at `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-write` whose profile name is `k8s-deny-write` and that **denies all writes** under `/etc/secret-data/`, then load it with `apparmor_parser`.

Target: file `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-write` on `$W1` contains `profile k8s-deny-write` and a `deny /etc/secret-data/** w,` rule.
questions.hint: Pipe a heredoc into `docker exec -i "$W1" tee /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-write`. Body: `#include <tunables/global>` then `profile k8s-deny-write flags=(attach_disconnected) { #include <abstractions/base>` + `file,` + `deny /etc/secret-data/** w,` + `}`. Load: `docker exec "$W1" apparmor_parser -r -W /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-write`.

verification.description: /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-write on $W1 has profile name k8s-deny-write + deny-write rule

questions.title: Reference the profile from a pod (Localhost)
questions.teach:
A container requests a loaded profile via `securityContext.appArmorProfile` (GA in 1.30+). Use `type: Localhost` with `localhostProfile: <profile-name>` — the value is the **profile name**, never a file path.

**Gotcha:** `Localhost` only works if that profile is loaded on the node the pod lands on — here we pin with `nodeName: $W1`. If the profile is missing on that node, the pod will not start.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `cks-apparmor`, create pod `confined` pinned to node `$W1`, image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`, container name `hello`, referencing the **Localhost** profile `k8s-deny-write`.

Target: pod `confined` is on `$W1` and container `hello` has `appArmorProfile.type: Localhost`, `localhostProfile: k8s-deny-write`.
questions.hint: Set `spec.containers[0].securityContext.appArmorProfile: { type: Localhost, localhostProfile: k8s-deny-write }` and `spec.nodeName: $W1`. (The equivalent beta annotation is `container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/hello: localhost/k8s-deny-write`.)
questions.solution:
cat <<YAML | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: confined
  namespace: cks-apparmor
spec:
  nodeName: $W1
  containers:
  - name: hello
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:
      appArmorProfile:
        type: Localhost
        localhostProfile: k8s-deny-write
YAML

verification.description: pod 'confined' on $W1, container hello → Localhost profile k8s-deny-write

questions.title: Prove the confinement blocks a write
questions.teach:
On an AppArmor-capable node an enforce-mode profile actually **blocks** the denied action: `kubectl exec confined -- sh -c 'touch /etc/secret-data/x'` returns `Permission denied`. Capture that proof so it can be graded.

**Gotcha:** the rule is path-specific — test the **protected** path (`/etc/secret-data/`), not `/tmp` (which the profile allows) or you'll see no denial.
questions.prompt:
Attempt a write to the **protected** path inside `confined` (`touch /etc/secret-data/x`) and capture its output into a ConfigMap `apparmor-proof` (key `result`) in `cks-apparmor`. The `confined` pod from Step 2 must stay bound to `k8s-deny-write`.

Target: ConfigMap `apparmor-proof` key `result` contains `Permission denied`, AND `confined` still references `k8s-deny-write`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n cks-apparmor create configmap apparmor-proof --from-literal=result="$(kubectl -n cks-apparmor exec confined -- sh -c 'touch /etc/secret-data/x' 2>&1)"`. Write to the denied path `/etc/secret-data/`, not `/tmp`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n cks-apparmor create configmap apparmor-proof \
  --from-literal=result="$(kubectl -n cks-apparmor exec confined -- sh -c 'touch /etc/secret-data/x' 2>&1)"
# on an AppArmor host: touch: /etc/secret-data/x: Permission denied

verification.description: apparmor-proof.result contains 'Permission denied' AND confined still bound to k8s-deny-write

questions.title: Contrast: an Unconfined pod
questions.teach:
To see what AppArmor buys you, compare. A container with `appArmorProfile.type: Unconfined` runs with **no** AppArmor confinement — the same write to `/etc/secret-data/` succeeds there while `confined` blocks it. Confinement is deliberate and per-container.

**Gotcha:** `Unconfined` is an explicit opt-out, distinct from simply omitting the field (which inherits the runtime default). Here we require the explicit `Unconfined` type.
questions.prompt:
In `cks-apparmor`, create pod `unconfined` on node `$W1`, image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`, container `hello`, with `appArmorProfile.type: Unconfined`.

Target: `unconfined`'s container `hello` has `appArmorProfile.type: Unconfined` (and does NOT reference k8s-deny-write).
questions.solution:
cat <<YAML | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: unconfined
  namespace: cks-apparmor
spec:
  nodeName: $W1
  containers:
  - name: hello
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:
      appArmorProfile:
        type: Unconfined
YAML

questions.title: RuntimeDefault at the pod level
questions.teach:
`appArmorProfile` can sit at the **pod** level (`spec.securityContext`) to set a default for all its containers. `type: RuntimeDefault` applies the container runtime's built-in default profile — no node file or `apparmor_parser` needed.

**Gotcha:** `RuntimeDefault` takes **no** `localhostProfile`; a container-level `appArmorProfile` overrides the pod-level default for that container.
questions.prompt:
In `cks-apparmor`, create pod `rtdefault` on node `$W1`, image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`, container `hello`, with **pod-level** `appArmorProfile.type: RuntimeDefault`.

Target: `rtdefault` has `spec.securityContext.appArmorProfile.type: RuntimeDefault`.
questions.hint: Put it on the pod, not the container: `spec.securityContext.appArmorProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault }`. No `localhostProfile` for RuntimeDefault.
questions.solution:
cat <<YAML | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: rtdefault
  namespace: cks-apparmor
spec:
  nodeName: $W1
  securityContext:
    appArmorProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
  - name: hello
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
YAML

questions.title: Load a second, stricter profile (deny network)
questions.teach:
AppArmor rules go beyond files: `deny network,` blocks all socket use. Write a second profile `k8s-deny-net` and load it alongside the first — a node can hold many loaded profiles, each tracked by its own profile name.

**Gotcha:** reloading one profile with `apparmor_parser -r` does not touch others; use `-R` to **remove** a profile. Loading a new file never un-loads `k8s-deny-write`.
questions.prompt:
On `$W1`, write `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-net` (profile name `k8s-deny-net`) that **denies all network access** (`deny network,`), and load it with `apparmor_parser`. Leave `k8s-deny-write` loaded.

Target: file `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-net` on `$W1` has `profile k8s-deny-net` and a `deny network,` rule.
questions.hint: Same heredoc-into-tee approach as Step 1. Body: `profile k8s-deny-net flags=(attach_disconnected) { #include <abstractions/base>` + `network,` + `deny network,` + `}`. Load with `apparmor_parser -r -W`.

verification.description: /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-net on $W1 has profile name k8s-deny-net + deny network rule

questions.title: Bind the stricter profile to a pod
questions.teach:
Each loaded profile is referenced by name. Point a pod at `k8s-deny-net` the same way as `k8s-deny-write`: `type: Localhost`, `localhostProfile: k8s-deny-net`, pinned to the node where it is loaded.

**Gotcha:** `localhostProfile` is a bare profile name — not `localhost/k8s-deny-net` and not a file path. The `localhost/` prefix belongs only to the old beta annotation.
questions.prompt:
In `cks-apparmor`, create pod `netlocked` on node `$W1`, image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`, container `hello`, referencing Localhost profile `k8s-deny-net`.

Target: pod `netlocked` on `$W1`, container `hello` has `appArmorProfile.type: Localhost`, `localhostProfile: k8s-deny-net`.
questions.hint: Identical shape to Step 2 but `localhostProfile: k8s-deny-net`. The value is the bare profile name (no `localhost/` prefix).
questions.solution:
cat <<YAML | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: netlocked
  namespace: cks-apparmor
spec:
  nodeName: $W1
  containers:
  - name: hello
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:
      appArmorProfile:
        type: Localhost
        localhostProfile: k8s-deny-net
YAML

verification.description: pod 'netlocked' on $W1, container hello → Localhost profile k8s-deny-net

questions.title: Diagnose & fix: a pod stuck on a missing profile
questions.teach:
A pod requesting `type: Localhost` with a profile that is **not loaded on its node** will not start — the kubelet rejects it (on an AppArmor host the pod is `Blocked`/fails scheduling). `kubectl describe pod` shows the AppArmor error naming the missing profile.

**Gotcha:** fix it at the **node**, not the pod — write and load that exact profile name with `apparmor_parser`; don't just delete and rebuild the pod.
questions.prompt:
Pod `broken-aa` in `cks-apparmor` is pinned to `$W1` and references Localhost profile `k8s-audit-write`, but that profile was never written or loaded on `$W1`. Diagnose and fix so the referenced profile exists and is loaded. Create the profile file at `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-audit-write` (profile name `k8s-audit-write`) denying writes under `/etc/secret-data/`, and load it. Do not delete the pod.

Target: file `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-audit-write` on `$W1` has `profile k8s-audit-write` + a deny-write rule for `/etc/secret-data/`, AND `broken-aa` still references it.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n cks-apparmor describe pod broken-aa` shows the missing-profile error. Write `/etc/apparmor.d/k8s-audit-write` (profile name `k8s-audit-write`, `deny /etc/secret-data/** w,`) via `docker exec -i "$W1" tee ...`, then `docker exec "$W1" apparmor_parser -r -W /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-audit-write`.

verification.description: k8s-audit-write profile written + loaded on $W1 AND broken-aa still references it
